chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job, the guard card and the post

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What a security officer does, and does not do
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the main duties of a security officer and the limits of a guard's authority.
This lesson builds toward: Given a conflict, theft or emergency situation, you will choose the observe-and-report action that stays within a guard's authority, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right, with emergency calls made first.
A security officer protects people and property. The everyday work is to be seen, watch, control who comes in, patrol, help people, answer alarms, and write down what happens. Being visible and alert prevents many problems before they start.
A security officer is not a police officer. In most states a guard has the same power to arrest as any private person, and no more. Most employers tell officers to "observe and report": watch carefully, call the police or a supervisor, and write it down, instead of chasing or grabbing people.
Your employer's rules (the post orders) can be stricter than the law. If the post orders say "do not detain", you do not detain, even if the law would allow it. Going beyond your orders can get you fired, sued or hurt.
Customer service is half the job. You give directions, help lost visitors and stay polite with angry people. Officers who are calm, on time and good at writing reports are the ones who get promoted.
Words to know:
- Security officer: a person paid to protect people and property; also called a security guard.
- Observe and report: watch, call for help and write it down, without getting physically involved.
- Post orders: the written instructions for one site: what to check, when, and what to do.
- Detain: to stop someone from leaving. Guards should only do it if the law and their post orders allow it.
- Deter: to stop a problem before it starts, for example by being seen.
Official sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Security guards and gambling surveillance officers (how to become one)
- California BSIS: Power to Arrest training manual
Try it now: Draw two columns on paper: "A guard does" and "A guard does not". Put each of these in a column: patrol the parking lot, search a person's bag by force, give a visitor directions, chase a shoplifter into the street, call 911 for a fight, write a report, handcuff someone because the post orders say observe and report. Then write one sentence on why.
You can now explain what a security officer does and the limits of a guard's authority.

check.q: What do most employers mean by "observe and report"?
options: Watch, call for help and write it down
Arrest people for any rule broken
check.why: Observe and report means you watch, call the police or a supervisor, and document, without physical involvement.

check.q: The law might allow a private arrest, but your post orders say "do not detain". What do you do?
options: Ask the suspect what they prefer
Follow the post orders: observe, call and report
check.why: Post orders can be stricter than the law, and you must follow them.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Getting your guard card: how state licensing works
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find your state's licensing agency and list the steps to get a guard card.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state's official licensing page, you will list the steps to get a guard card in your state, naming the agency, the age rule, the background check and the training required before and after you are licensed.
Most states license security guards through a state agency. The common pattern: be at least 18, pass a criminal background check with fingerprints, and finish training with an approved school or employer. Many states also need training every year. The names differ: a "guard card", "registration" or "Class D license".
California is our checked example. The agency is the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services (BSIS). You must be at least 18, pass a Department of Justice and FBI background check through Live Scan fingerprints, and finish the Power to Arrest training before the registration is issued. Then you finish 32 hours of security officer skills training within the first 6 months, and 8 hours of continuing training every year. You apply online in BreEZe or by mail, and you carry your card on duty.
Other states have their own agency, for example the New York Department of State, the Texas Department of Public Safety's Private Security Program, and Florida's Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, Division of Licensing. Look up your own state's official page for the current training hours, fees and forms. Do not trust a training ad for the rules.
If you have a criminal record: each state decides which records matter. Answer every question honestly, because a false answer can itself lead to a denial. A reentry program or legal aid office can help you read your state's rules.
Step by step:
- Search for your state's security guard licensing agency and open the official .gov page.
- Write down: minimum age, background check and fingerprint steps.
- Write the training required before you are licensed and after (first months, every year).
- Find the application (online or paper) and the fee page; don't guess the fee.
- Note how to renew and how long the license lasts.
Words to know:
- Guard card: the everyday name for a state security guard license or registration.
- BSIS: California's Bureau of Security and Investigative Services, which registers guards in California.
- Live Scan: electronic fingerprinting used for background checks in California and other states.
- Background check: a search of criminal records, often by the state and the FBI, before a license is issued.
- Continuing training: training you must keep doing after you are licensed, often every year.
Official sources:
- California BSIS: Security Guard Registration fact sheet
- California BSIS: Security guard training syllabus (courses and hours)
- New York Department of State: Security guard licensing
- Texas Department of Public Safety: Private Security Program
- Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services: Division of Licensing (Class D security officer)
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Security guards and gambling surveillance officers (how to become one)
Try it now: Open your state's official licensing page (or California's BSIS fact sheet if you are practicing). On paper, write your state's guard card steps in order: agency, age, background check, training before the card, training after, how to apply, and the page address.
You can now find your state's licensing agency and list the steps to get a guard card.

check.q: In California, which training must be finished before the guard registration is issued?
check.why: BSIS says Power to Arrest training must be completed before the registration is issued.

check.q: A training ad says your state needs only a 2-hour online class. What do you do?
options: Check the state agency's official page
check.why: Rules change and differ by state; only the official agency page is reliable.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Post orders, patrol and access control
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Carry out a patrol and an entrance check by following written post orders.
This lesson builds toward: Given a set of post orders, you will carry out a patrol and an access-control check, covering every point in the post orders and logging what you saw and did with the time.
Every site has post orders. They tell you your hours, where to patrol and how often, which doors to check, who may come in, what to do in an alarm, and who to call. Read them at the start of every shift, and ask your supervisor about anything unclear.
On patrol, vary your timing so nobody can predict you. Use your senses: look for open doors, broken locks, leaks, smoke, blocked fire exits, lights out and people where they should not be. Write each check in your daily activity log with the time.
Access control means only the right people get in. Check badges or ID the way the post orders say, sign visitors in and out, give visitor passes, and never let someone follow you through a locked door (tailgating). Be polite and firm: "I'm sorry, I need to see your badge."
Use your radio or phone the way the site says: short, clear messages with your location. At shift change, tell the next officer what is open and pass on the log.
Step by step:
- Read the post orders and the last shift's log.
- Check your radio or phone and keys.
- Patrol every point in the post orders, at varied times.
- At the entrance: check ID or badge, sign visitors in, stop tailgating.
- Log each check and anything unusual with the time.
- Brief the next officer at shift change.
Words to know:
- Patrol: walking or driving around a site on a route to look for problems.
- Access control: making sure only allowed people and vehicles get in.
- Tailgating: someone following an allowed person through a locked door without showing ID.
- Daily activity log: the officer's written record of each check and event during a shift, with times.
Official sources:
- California BSIS: Security guard training syllabus (courses and hours)
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Security guards and gambling surveillance officers (how to become one)
Try it now: Pick a practice post: your apartment building, a library or a store you know. Write five lines of post orders for it (hours, patrol points, entrance rule, who to call). Then write a one-hour daily activity log for that post with at least four timed entries, including one problem you found and what you did.
You can now carry out a patrol and an entrance check from written post orders and log them.

check.q: Why should you vary the time of your patrols?
options: So nobody can predict when you will come by
check.why: Predictable patrols are easy for a wrongdoer to avoid; varied times deter problems.

check.q: A person without a badge walks in right behind an employee. What is this?
check.why: Tailgating is following someone through a controlled door without showing ID.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Conflict, emergencies, reports and getting hired

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Calming conflict, use of force and emergencies
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose a calm, safe response to a conflict, a theft or an emergency.
This lesson builds toward: Given a conflict, theft or emergency situation, you will choose the observe-and-report action that stays within a guard's authority, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right, with emergency calls made first.
Most conflict can be calmed with words. Keep a safe distance, stand at an angle, keep your hands open and visible, and speak slowly and quietly. Listen, use the person's name if you know it, and offer a choice: "You can wait here or I can call your manager." Do not argue, touch or block someone in.
Use of force is the most serious part of the job. States teach it in their training (California requires Appropriate Use of Force and Power to Arrest courses). The rule to remember: only the force the law and your post orders allow, only when needed, and stop as soon as it is not. Most unarmed officers are told to leave and call the police instead.
Theft: watch, remember the description, call the police or your supervisor as your orders say, and do not chase into the street or a parking lot. Your safety and others' matter more than goods.
Emergencies: for fire, medical emergencies, fights or weapons, call 911 (or your local emergency number) first, then follow the site's emergency plan: alert people, guide them to exits, meet the responders and tell them what you saw. First aid and CPR are learned and certified in person with a qualified instructor, for example from the American Red Cross or the American Heart Association.
Step by step:
- Check: is anyone in danger? If yes, call 911 first.
- Keep a safe distance and an escape route.
- Speak calmly; listen; offer a choice.
- If it is not calming down, step back and call police or your supervisor.
- Follow the site's emergency plan; guide people out; meet responders.
- Write it down as soon as it is safe.
Words to know:
- De-escalation: using calm words and body language to lower someone's anger.
- Use of force: any physical action to control a person; guards may only use what the law and their orders allow.
- Emergency plan: the site's written steps for fire, medical events, weapons and evacuation.
- Evacuation: getting everyone out of a building safely.
Official sources:
- California BSIS: Security guard training syllabus (courses and hours)
- California BSIS: Power to Arrest training manual
Try it now: Practice with a friend or in a mirror. Scene: a visitor is shouting at the front desk because they cannot go up without a badge. Say out loud three calm sentences, including one choice you offer. Then write the point at which you would step back and call your supervisor or the police.
You can now choose a calm, safe response to a conflict, a theft or an emergency, staying within your authority.

check.q: A person collapses in the lobby and is not breathing normally. What do you do first?
options: Call 911, then follow the emergency plan
check.why: In a medical emergency you call 911 (or your local number) first.

check.q: A shoplifter runs out to the parking lot with goods. Your orders say observe and report. What do you do?
options: Note the description and direction and call as your orders say
check.why: You stay safe, gather facts and call; goods are not worth a life.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Observe, describe and write the incident report
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a factual incident report that answers who, what, when, where and how.
This lesson builds toward: After watching or reading about an incident, you will write a factual incident report, answering who, what, when, where and how, using facts, not opinions, in time order.
Your report may be read by your supervisor, the client, an insurance company, the police or a court, sometimes months later. A good report lets a stranger see exactly what happened. Many officers lose credibility because their reports are vague.
Write facts, not opinions. Not "he was drunk" but "he smelled of alcohol, swayed and slurred his words". Not "a suspicious guy" but "a man about 30, about 6 feet, red hooded jacket, black backpack, walked around the parked cars and tried two door handles".
Answer who, what, when, where and how, in time order. Give the date and exact times, the exact place, the people involved and witnesses, what you saw and heard yourself, what you did, and who you called and when. Write the exact words people said in quotes.
Write it as soon as it is safe, while you remember. Use first person ("I saw"), short sentences and correct names. Do not guess, add or leave things out. If you make a mistake, correct it the way your employer says; never change a report later to make it look better.
Step by step:
- Date, time and exact place.
- Who: you, the people involved, witnesses (names and descriptions).
- What happened, in time order, with what you saw and heard yourself.
- What you did and who you called, with times.
- Exact words in quotes; facts, not opinions.
- Read it again; sign it as your employer requires.
Words to know:
- Incident report: a written, factual record of an event such as a theft, injury, fight or alarm.
- Witness: a person who saw or heard what happened.
- Fact: something you saw, heard or measured yourself.
- Opinion: what you think or guess, such as "he looked guilty".
Official sources:
- California BSIS: Security guard training syllabus (courses and hours)
Try it now: Watch any 2-minute public scene (a busy street, a store entrance or a short video with no sound). Then write a practice incident report: date, time, place, people described by facts, what happened in time order, and what you would have done and who you would have called. Underline any opinion words and rewrite them as facts.
You can now write a factual incident report that answers who, what, when, where and how.

check.q: Which sentence belongs in an incident report?
options: The man looked like a thief.
At 9:42 p.m. a man in a red jacket tried two car door handles in Row C.
check.why: It gives time, place, description and action as facts, not opinions.

check.q: When should you write the report?
options: As soon as it is safe, while you remember
After talking to everyone to agree on a story
check.why: Writing soon keeps the details accurate.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your guard card plan and getting hired
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a dated plan to finish training, apply for the guard card and get hired.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state's rules and local job listings, you will write a dated plan to get licensed and hired, with dates for training, fingerprints, application and job applications, and an honest résumé line. Using your state's official licensing page, you will list the steps to get a guard card in your state, naming the agency, the age rule, the background check and the training required before and after you are licensed.
Turn your state's steps into dates. For example: week 1, find an approved training school or an employer that trains new officers; week 2, finish the training required before the card; week 3, get fingerprinted and apply; then apply for jobs while the agency processes your application. In California, BSIS says to allow about 4 to 6 weeks for processing, and it can take longer.
Many security companies hire people and help them through the training. Look on job boards, at your local American Job Center or workforce center, and on company websites. Check that a training school is approved by your state (California lets you verify a license online). Be wary of anyone who promises a "guaranteed" license.
Your résumé: be honest. Before you are licensed, write "Completed security officer preparation course; guard card application in progress". Name the skills: report writing, customer service, patrol, staying calm under pressure. Veterans: describe military police, guard duty or watch-standing in everyday words.
Practice interview answers: "How would you handle an angry visitor?" and "What would you do if you saw a theft?" Use what you learned: stay calm, observe and report, call for help, write it down.
Step by step:
- Copy your state's guard card steps from Lesson 2.
- Put a date next to each step.
- List three employers or approved schools near you.
- Write an honest résumé line and three skills.
- Practice two interview answers out loud.
Words to know:
- Approved school: a training provider your state allows to give the required guard training.
- American Job Center: a free U.S. public office that helps with job search and training.
- Processing time: how long the agency takes to review your application and background check.
Official sources:
- California BSIS: Security Guard Registration fact sheet
- California Department of Consumer Affairs: Verify a license
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Security guards and gambling surveillance officers (how to become one)
Try it now: Make your guard card plan on one page: each step from your state's page with a date, three local employers or approved schools, an honest résumé line, and your answers to the two interview questions. Put it with your checklist and practice report: that is your readiness packet.
You can now write a dated plan to get your guard card and a job, with an honest résumé line.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds State guard card steps Missing the agency, the background check or the training, or uses a training ad instead of the official page. Lists the agency, age, background check, training before and after licensing, how to apply, and the official page address. Adds renewal rules and how to verify a school or license. Patrol and access checklist Missing patrol points, the entrance rule or the log. Covers every point in the practice post orders and includes a timed log with at least four entries. Adds the shift handover and a plan for tailgating. Observe-and-report pocket card Includes chasing, force beyond the orders, or no 911-first step. Shows calm words, when to step back and call, no chasing, and 911 first in emergencies. Adds the site's emergency plan steps and what to tell responders. Practice incident report Vague, has opinions, or missing times or place. Answers who, what, when, where and how in time order with facts and exact quotes. Descriptions are detailed enough for a stranger to identify people and places. Dated plan and résumé line No dates, or claims a license not yet held. Dates for each step, three local employers or approved schools, an honest résumé line. Includes practiced answers to two interview questions. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check again.

check.q: You have finished this course but your guard card has not been issued. Which résumé line is honest?
options: "Completed security officer preparation course; guard card application in progress"
check.why: It says exactly what you have done without claiming a license you do not hold.

check.q: How can you check that a training school or license is real in California?
options: Use the state's online license verification
check.why: California's Department of Consumer Affairs lets you verify licenses online.
